newsitem.title: IRAN: Efforts under way to return EU envoys to Tehran.
newsitem.headline: Efforts under way to return EU envoys to Tehran.

text.p: Iran and the European Union are engaged in last-minute efforts to try to get EU ambassadors back to Tehran in time for the new president's swearing-in ceremony on Monday, diplomats said on Sunday.

They said the efforts aimed at timing the return so that EU ambassadors could attend the oath-taking ceremony of President Mohammad Khatami in parliament, but that Iran had rejected the idea of a collective return of envoys on the same aircraft.
Khatami was formally confirmed as president by supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on Sunday but efforts to get the EU envoys back in time for that ceremony failed.

EU states except for Greece recalled their ambassadors from Tehran after a German court concluded in April that Iran's top leaders had ordered the 1992 assassination of four Iranian Kurdish dissidents in a Berlin restaurant.

Iran is insisting that the German ambassador, Horst Beschmann, should be the last to arrive and has rejected a European offer that he be the last to step off a plane carrying all the envoys to Tehran, the diplomats said.

"The Iranians are insisting that the German envoy be the last one to arrive. There are still some efforts for tomorrow Monday," an Arab ambassador told Reuters. "There is still a chance...They could come," he added.
"Certainly the idea of the ambassadors' joint return has fallen through," a Western diplomat in Tehran said.
The diplomats said there was still a slim chance that a compromise would be reached by which the ambassadors would arrive separately, the German envoy being the last.
They said Iran had sent invitations to foreign embassies in Tehran, including those of the EU states, addressed to the ambassadors to attend Sunday's and Monday's ceremonies.
When the EU envoys left Tehran the 15-nation bloc also suspended all ministerial contacts with Tehran as well as its policy of "critical dialogue" with Iran.
Iran, which has repeatedly denied involvement in the Berlin killings, withdrew its ambassadors from EU capitals.
But when the EU countries later decided to send their ambassadors back to Tehran, Khamenei said the German ambassador was not welcome in Tehran.
In Bonn, Germany's Foreign Ministry said the new initiatives to return European ambassadors to Tehran did not alter its understanding of current EU policy on the issue.

"The Luxembourg (European Union) presidency has said it has tried to bring about the return of EU ambassadors to Tehran without discrimination and that this effort has failed. The ball is in Tehran's court," a spokesman said.
Iran's outgoing President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani on Saturday indicated the EU envoys may return to Tehran but Bonn's envoy must be the last.

Asked to comment on indications EU countries were ready to send their envoys back to Iran, Rafsanjani said: "That is true. They are now ready to return since the leader of the revolution (Khamenei) said that they can do so. Germany must return after everyone else."
He said the European states wanted to return together but that Iran would deal with each country separately.

"You must sort yourself out. If you wish to work with Iran, you should not resort to such ploys," Rafsanjani said. "The (European countries) thought that we will retreat in the face of this pressure and make concessions, but they realised that Iran is far stronger than to be frightened by such ploys," he said.
"However, this has not ended yet. The issue can go on, but eventually the Europeans must accept that they have made a mistake," he added.
